account: The RL weight change that matters is low-rank: the top-8 singular directions of each matrix's RL-minus-base difference hold about 13 % of its norm (as much under an LM-judge reward, 0.127, as under the math reward, 0.135, against 0.030 for Think-SFT), and they sit on input and output directions the base already uses for step-by-step text, which Think-SFT, Code-RL and Math 3.0 also move along (Think-SFT 4.8x chance; Math 3.1's per-matrix share pattern follows Think-SFT's, rho 0.59, not IF-RL's, rho -0.01), so on-policy RL picks the place from the base and the reward sets mainly how far to move along it.

In behaviour this change does two things in order: by RL step 100 it switches most samples, one sample at a time, to the deliberative opening that the three-token cue selects (step-100 answers 1.15x the cued base's length, same cap-hit rate, same +7-point vote-of-4 gain, and the cue adds only 8.5 of 500); after that it lowers the per-step slip rate on that same route and moves its route choice toward RL's own (the edit's wrong answers agree with RL's by 0.29 more than the base's do), so final RL hits the cap 2.9 points less often, writes 1.6x longer answers, and its samples agree so much that a vote gains only 2.8 points.

The untrained base changed only at inference gets the switch in full (a plain answer that happens to open deliberatively is right as often as a cued one, -0.03; T 1.0 removes the loops that fill 52-63 % of long T 0.6 attempts) and gets back part of the slip reduction by voting, because its wrong answers scatter (pairwise agreement 0.26; a vote with the real wrong answers beats one with them merged by 0.07-0.11), and that is the roughly 18 of 29 points it reaches.

The remaining ~11 points are problems where the base has no right answer in 4 samples (26 of the 36 problems RL's vote wins), which no prompt, sampling or vote can select; adding the Math 3.1 top-8 directions at 1.5x recovers them almost entirely (0.88 of RL's per-sample edge there; 203 vs RL 205 of 328 per sample on hard328, against 164 for the cued base; vote-of-4 equal to RL's within 0.1 point), while random rank-8 edits at any scale from -1x to 3x stay at the base's 159-167.

The gain lives in few directions in layers 0-21 and saturates at RL's level: layers 0-10 or 11-21 alone at 1.5x each give about half (183-184), layers 22-31 give nothing and hurt at 3x (166, then 155), top-1 gives about half (181) and drops at 3x (168), Math 3.0's top-8 at 1x gives about half (182), IF-RL's top-8 and Think-SFT's top-8 at tiny scale give nothing (155-156), and adding directions to a model that already has the switch and the slip reduction (RL, Think-SFT, theta >= 0.5) adds nothing beyond that model's own score (193-197 onto RL, 232 onto Think-SFT = Think-SFT's 230, theta 0.5 452 vs RL 457 on MATH-500).

At 1x the edit acts as a per-sample route lottery more than a graded shift (on cued-solved problems m21's deliberative answers beat its non-deliberative ones by 0.57, and 41 % of its right answers stay plain-short), and on code the Code-RL top-8 1.5x edit raises the pass rate 7 points over a random edit by picking programs the base already writes in other samples (75 % of its fixes), not by copying RL-Code's outcomes (0.45 on problems RL-Code fails, as base resamples get); Math's directions add only 1.5 points on code.
